notes: Asylum permission-to-appeal appeal; Pill LJ restored the IAT on application of Hayser country guidance to adjudicator fact findings.

enrichment.short_title: Bozkurt: application of Turkish country conditions to Alevi Kurd asylum facts
key_facts: Mr Cafer Bozkurt, an Alevi Kurd from Tunceli, claimed asylum after leaving Turkey following attendance at a cousin's funeral linked to TKPML.
The adjudicator found past ill-treatment but rejected the account as lacking credibility and held no real risk of persecution on return.
The Immigration Appeal Tribunal refused permission to appeal; Beatson J quashed that refusal, relying on post-determination Hayser country guidance on GBTS entry checks.
The Home Office appealed, contending the adjudicator had correctly applied general country information to the particular facts.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal appeal against a High Court decision quashing the IAT's refusal of permission to appeal from an asylum adjudicator's determination.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed with costs; the adjudicator and Tribunal did not err in law and Beatson J's quashing order was set aside.
enrichment.ratio: An appellate court should not interfere with an adjudicator's application of general country conditions to particular facts unless the process of reasoning requires a different view; Hayser risk factors are an aide-memoire, not a mandatory checklist, and their absence from a reasoned determination is not necessarily an error.
legal_issues: Whether the adjudicator erred in applying Turkish country conditions to the claimant's accepted facts
Whether the Tribunal erred in refusing permission to appeal
The correct test for detecting error following Indrakumar and Subesh
Whether Hayser guidelines required explicit application in every case

Subesh v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2004] EWCA Civ 56
Hayser v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2002] UKIAT 07083

notes: Princess Diana coaching videotapes; Peter Smith J held police had no lawful basis to retain a copy after Burrell acquittal.

enrichment.short_title: Settelen v Met Police: delivery up of Princess Diana coaching videotape copy
key_facts: Mr Settelen recorded Princess Diana during speech coaching sessions and claimed ownership and copyright in the videotapes left with the Princess.
Six tapes were found at Paul Burrell's home after his acquittal on unrelated theft charges; the police retained them amid competing claims with the Princess's estate.
After the estate renounced its claim, the police returned originals but secretly copied one tape for investigation into Diana's and a protection officer's deaths.
Settelen sought delivery up of the copy; the police conceded delivery subject to undertakings but disputed entitlement and sought costs.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Urgent without-notice application for delivery up and information concerning a police-held copy videotape, with costs determined on the merits.
enrichment.outcome: Claimants entitled to delivery up of the copy tape on undertakings; the police ordered to pay the claimants' costs.
enrichment.ratio: After the purpose of seizure ceased with Burrell's acquittal, neither PACE section 22 nor Ghani v Jones common-law retention justified keeping a third party's property; where undertakings adequately preserve evidence for ongoing investigations, retention of a copy is not necessary in all the circumstances.
legal_issues: Whether the police could retain a copy tape under sections 19 and 22 PACE after the criminal investigation ended
Whether common-law retention powers applied against the true owner
Whether a balancing exercise under section 22 permitted retention for a separate death investigation
Costs where delivery was conceded but entitlement was disputed

notes: Long TCC trial on defective polycarbonate floodlight housings; Anglo liable to Rowan but BIP not liable upstream.

enrichment.short_title: Trac Time v Rowan: defective reprocessed polycarbonate floodlight housings
key_facts: Trac supplied floodlights whose polycarbonate housings were injection-moulded by Rowan (later Moss) from material sourced via Anglo from Regent/BIP.
Low-grade reprocessed polycarbonate with excessive melt volume rate caused brittle housings that cracked; over 60,000 lights were sold before defects surfaced in October 2001.
Trac claimed past and future return losses from Rowan; Rowan claimed against Anglo; Anglo claimed against Regent/BIP in a multi-party supply chain trial.
Expert evidence showed all Anglo-period supplies failed specification and satisfactory quality requirements.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Multi-party Technology and Construction Court trial on breach of contract, specification, causation and quantum across a four-link supply chain.
enrichment.outcome: Rowan/Moss liable to Trac and Anglo liable to Rowan for supplying non-conforming polycarbonate; BIP not held in breach to Anglo; damages figures to be finalised on stated principles.
enrichment.ratio: Where moulded goods must correspond with an agreed polycarbonate specification, supply of reprocessed material exceeding MVR limits breaches description, satisfactory quality and fitness for purpose under the Sale of Goods Act; downstream processing defects do not break causation if the raw material was fundamentally unsuitable.
legal_issues: Whether housings and raw polycarbonate complied with express and implied contractual specifications
Causation where Rowan's processing may have contributed to cracking
Whether BIP inherited Regent's contractual liability on takeover
Quantum of past and future returns, associated costs and lost profits

notes: Post-trial costs judgment; Woolf LJ held defendant successful and penalised claimant for rejecting admissible without-prejudice offer.

enrichment.short_title: Grosvenor v High-Point Rendel: costs after recovering 2% of commission claim
key_facts: Grosvenor claimed substantial sales commissions from High-Point Rendel but recovered only £1,644.38 including VAT and interest, about 2% of the gross claim.
The claimant had rejected a £25,000 inclusive offer dated 14 January 2004 and made its own excessive without-prejudice offers.
The defendant succeeded on most issues including pre- and post-August 2000 commission, post-termination commission and major Pfizer and BTP claims.
The claimant falsely asserted the January offer was never received before withdrawing that point.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Written submissions on costs following a Commercial Court trial judgment on commission entitlement.
enrichment.outcome: Issue-based costs order favouring the defendant: limited recovery for the claimant pre-offer; thereafter each party bears own costs and the defendant recovers 75% of its costs.
enrichment.ratio: Where issues are clear and discrete, courts should make issue-based costs orders rather than blindly follow the event; an admissible non-Part 36 offer may significantly affect costs even without Part 36 consequences, especially where rejection was unreasonable.
legal_issues: Who was the successful party for costs purposes
Whether an issue-based costs order was appropriate
Effect of admissible without-prejudice offers under CPR 44.3
Whether the claimant's conduct warranted depriving it of costs

notes: Age-dispute JR for Angolan asylum seeker; Jackson J quashed unfair Enfield assessment ignoring paediatric and psychiatric evidence.

enrichment.short_title: R (C) v Enfield: judicial review of age assessment for unaccompanied asylum seeker
key_facts: C, an Angolan unaccompanied asylum seeker, claimed to have been born on 12 February 1987 and to be a child on arrival.
Enfield assessed her as 18+ on 23 April 2004 despite paediatric, psychological and psychiatric reports supporting age 17 and severe PTSD.
An immigration adjudicator accepted her date of birth and allowed a human rights appeal; the Secretary of State accepted she was born in February 1987.
The council's interview was hostile, ignored Dr Michie's report and failed to ask why she knew her date of birth.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Substantive judicial review of local authority age assessments refusing Children Act support to an unaccompanied minor.
enrichment.outcome: Claim succeeded; the 23 April 2004 assessment was quashed and a fresh assessment ordered with continued support pending reassessment.
enrichment.ratio: Age assessments must be fair and comply with published guidance; failure to consider relevant medical and psychiatric evidence, and unduly hostile questioning of a vulnerable traumatised child, renders an assessment unlawful even where the authority may lawfully disagree with other decision-makers.
legal_issues: Whether assessors failed to ask why the claimant asserted her date of birth
Whether Dr Michie's paediatric report was properly considered
Whether Child Guidance and psychiatric evidence was ignored
Whether the interview breached fairness requirements in age-assessment guidance

notes: Post-appeal costs hearing in Raja/Van Hoogstraten litigation; Chadwick LJ ordered usual costs and £90,000 interim payment.

enrichment.short_title: Raja v Van Hoogstraten: costs and interim payment after sequestration appeal
key_facts: The Court of Appeal had set aside a writ of sequestration and discharge of Van Hoogstraten's defence based on a flawed contempt finding.
A separate Tombstone Ltd intervention appeal was left unresolved with no further order because the substantive ownership issue never arose.
The claimant resisted immediate payment of costs, arguing future abuse-of-process findings might affect entitlement.
Van Hoogstraten sought costs of appeals and post-August 2002 proceedings plus a £90,000 interim payment.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Further hearing to settle consequential costs and interim payment orders after substantive appellate judgments in high-value civil litigation.
enrichment.outcome: Van Hoogstraten awarded costs of the appeals and relevant proceedings below; interim payment of £90,000 within two months; Tombstone appeal disposed of by no further order.
enrichment.ratio: Under the CPR pay-as-you-go approach, a successful appellant is ordinarily entitled to immediate costs of discrete interlocutory success even where broader abuse issues remain live; a freezing order, not deferred costs payment, protects against dissipation.
legal_issues: Whether costs of successful sequestration appeals should be deferred pending possible future abuse findings
Whether costs below after the August 2002 freezing order should follow the appeal event
Appropriate interim payment on account of costs
What order should be made on Tombstone's late intervention appeal

notes: Landmark director disclosure duty appeal; Arden LJ upheld liability for non-disclosure and allowed apportionment claim.

enrichment.short_title: Item Software v Fassihi: director's duty to disclose own misconduct
key_facts: Mr Fassihi, a sales director of Item, secretly sought to divert the main Isograph distribution contract to his new company RAMS while involved in negotiations.
Item dismissed him and claimed damages for breach of fiduciary and employment duties including failure to disclose his misconduct.
The judge held non-disclosure was a further breach causing loss when Item lost the Isograph contract; Fassihi counterclaimed for salary to dismissal.
The apportionment issue concerned salary for 1-26 June 2000 paid monthly in arrears after summary dismissal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal on liability-only trial findings as to disclosure duties and entitlement to apportioned salary under the Apportionment Act 1870.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed on disclosure; appeal allowed on apportionment; a director's duty of loyalty requires disclosure of own misconduct and section 2 of the 1870 Act permits recovery of salary for the broken pay period.
enrichment.ratio: A director's core fiduciary duty of loyalty requires disclosure of his own disloyal misconduct affecting the company; Bell v Lever Bros does not exclude that duty, and the Apportionment Act 1870 overrides the common-law rule denying salary for an incomplete pay period after dismissal.
legal_issues: Whether a director owes a duty to disclose his own misconduct beyond Bell v Lever Bros
Whether non-disclosure of diversion of corporate opportunity caused recoverable loss
Whether the Apportionment Act 1870 applies to salary accrued before dismissal but payable later
Distinction between employee and fiduciary duties on disclosure

notes: Fletton brick render defect trial; Coulson J dismissed lease, tort and estoppel claims for limitation and no duty.

enrichment.short_title: HM v Ideal Homes: Fletton brick sulphate attack and failed render remedial scheme
key_facts: HM, freehold owner of Norway Dock flats, claimed £881,892 remedial costs for render failure caused by sulphate attack from Fletton bricks in external walls.
Ideal North West built the estate in 1989-91; Ideal Southern carried out a failed 1995-96 remedial scheme; Persimmon SE briefly assisted then withdrew in 2002.
Leases covenanting completion to approved plans contained no express quality obligations and excluded implied developer obligations in favour of lessees.
Expert advice did not identify Fletton bricks as the cause until January 2004.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Technology and Construction Court trial on implied lease covenants, negligence, limitation, estoppel and successor liability.
enrichment.outcome: All claims dismissed against Ideal North West, Ideal Southern and Persimmon SE; no implied terms in the leases, no tort duty for economic loss, claims time-barred and no recoverable loss identified.
enrichment.ratio: A developer's obligations as to construction quality owed to the original contract employer cannot be recreated by implying collateral warranties into leases peripheral to the developer; economic loss from defective building work is not recoverable in tort by subsequent freeholders, and abortive remedial costs—not full replacement cost—measure tort loss from a failed scheme.
legal_issues: Whether leases implied workmanlike construction and fitness covenants owed to the freehold owner
Whether builders owed a duty to prevent economic loss to subsequent owners
When limitation ran on contract and tort claims including section 14A
Whether Persimmon's 2002 involvement estopped limitation defences

notes: M6 Land Rover rollover appeal; Exel liable for negligent tyre assembly; apportionment adjusted to equal blame.

enrichment.short_title: Exel v Curran: under-inflated tyres and negligent wheel assembly on M6
key_facts: A Land Rover Defender with twelve passengers rolled on the M6 after overtaking a coach, causing serious and fatal injuries.
Rear tyres were seriously under-inflated throughout the journey; Land Rover admitted that negligence contributed to the accident.
Exel had negligently assembled the front off-side tyre leaving grit that caused inner-tube failure and progressive deflation during the trip.
The judge acquitted driver Curran of negligence but held Exel two-thirds liable with Land Rover one-third.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against findings of driver negligence, causation of tyre failure and contributory negligence apportionment after a road traffic liability trial.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal largely dismissed on liability; allowed only on apportionment to 50/50 between Exel and Land Rover; Curran not negligent.
enrichment.ratio: A driver of a well-maintained company vehicle need not check tyre pressures before a journey; where under-inflated rear tyres create latent instability and a negligently assembled front tyre precipitates loss of control, both defects are equally causative and blameworthy for apportionment purposes.
legal_issues: Whether the driver was negligent in failing to check tyre pressures or heed instability
Whether Exel's negligent assembly caused pre-accident deflation of the front off-side tyre
Whether driving error rather than tyre defects initiated the loss of control
Correct apportionment between tyre assembler and fleet maintainer

notes: POCA restraint-order costs appeal; Scott Baker LJ held section 41(4) bars use of restrained funds for restraint-order legal expenses.

enrichment.short_title: S v Customs: restrained assets and legal expenses under POCA section 41
key_facts: Customs obtained an ex parte restraint order over Mr S's worldwide assets during a missing-trader VAT carousel fraud investigation.
The order purported to allow £750 for legal advice on the order itself, but Customs argued the court lacked jurisdiction to authorise such expenditure.
Mr S could not use restrained funds and was refused public funding, leaving him without representation to challenge draconian repatriation obligations.
Section 41(4) prohibits exceptions for legal expenses relating to the offence under investigation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with leave against refusal to vary a POCA restraint order to permit payment of legal expenses from restrained assets.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; section 41(4) precludes release of restrained funds for legal advice or representation relating to the restraint order; public funding is the intended route.
enrichment.ratio: Legal expenses 'relating to' the investigated offence under section 41(4) include costs of advising on and varying the restraint order itself; Parliament coupled that prohibition with public funding for restraint proceedings and inclusion of tainted-gift recipients to preserve realisable property for confiscation.
legal_issues: Whether section 41(4) bars use of restrained assets for legal expenses on the restraint order
Meaning of 'relate to an offence' in sections 41(4) and 41(5)
Whether denial of representation breaches Article 6 ECHR
Whether Article 1 Protocol 1 is infringed by temporary restraint
